lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic Cells: Structures and Differences

pages.body:
All living things are made of cells — from the tiniest bacterium to a blue whale. But not all cells are the same. Some bacteria are so simple that their entire cell contents float freely inside, with no internal compartments. Others — including every cell in your own body — are far more complex, with a distinct nucleus and specialised structures inside.

- What do you think are the most important parts of a cell?
- Why might cells need to have separate compartments inside them?
- Can you name any living thing that consists of only one cell?

> **DEFINITION** **Prokaryotic cell:** a cell that does NOT have a true, membrane-bound nucleus. The genetic material (DNA) is found loose in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid. Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller and simpler than eukaryotic cells. **Eukaryotic cell:** a cell that HAS a true, membrane-bound nucleus containing the DNA. Eukaryotic cells are generally larger and more complex, with many membrane-bound organelles. **Organelle:** a small, specialised structure inside a cell that performs a specific function, such as the mitochondrion (produces energy) or the ribosome (makes proteins). **Nucleus:** the membrane-bound control centre of a eukaryotic cell, containing the cell's DNA (genetic information).

pages.title: The prokaryotic cell
pages.body: Prokaryotic cells are the oldest and simplest type of cell. The word 'prokaryote' means 'before the nucleus'. Prokaryotic cells are typically much smaller than eukaryotic cells — most are between 1 and 10 micrometres in diameter. All bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes. Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria), which are found in ponds and rivers in Ghana, are also prokaryotes.

The key features of a prokaryotic cell are as follows. There is no nucleus — the DNA floats freely in the cytoplasm in a region called the nucleoid, which is not surrounded by a membrane. The cell has a cell membrane that controls what enters and leaves. Most prokaryotes also have a rigid cell wall surrounding the membrane, providing shape and protection. Ribosomes are present — these are tiny structures that make proteins. Some prokaryotes have a flagellum (a tail-like structure for movement) and some have pili (tiny hair-like projections for attachment). Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria or a nucleus.

pages.title: The eukaryotic cell
pages.body: Eukaryotic cells are larger and much more complex than prokaryotic cells. The word 'eukaryote' means 'true nucleus'. All plants, animals, fungi and protists (single-celled organisms like amoeba) are made of eukaryotic cells. Your own body is made entirely of eukaryotic cells.

The most important feature is the nucleus — a membrane-bound compartment containing the DNA. The membrane around the nucleus is called the nuclear membrane (or nuclear envelope). Inside the nucleus is the nucleolus, which makes ribosomal RNA. Outside the nucleus, the cytoplasm contains numerous specialised organelles. The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membranes involved in protein and lipid production. Mitochondria (singular: mitochondrion) produce energy from food by a process called cellular respiration — they are often called the 'powerhouses of the cell'. Ribosomes are present in both cell types and make proteins. Plant eukaryotic cells additionally have a cell wall (made of cellulose, unlike the bacterial cell wall), chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a large central vacuole.

pages.title: Comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
pages.body:
The single most important difference is the presence of a true, membrane-bound nucleus in eukaryotic cells. Prokaryotes have no such nucleus — their DNA is free in the cytoplasm. Eukaryotes are also much larger (typically 10 to 100 micrometres) compared to prokaryotes (1 to 10 micrometres). Eukaryotes have membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria; prokaryotes do not. Both types have a cell membrane and ribosomes, but the ribosomes differ in size. Both types can have a cell wall, but the chemical composition differs: bacteria use peptidoglycan while plant cells use cellulose.

> **Lesson 1 Assessment**

questions.q: Which of the following is the key difference between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
o: Eukaryotic cells are smaller than prokaryotic cells
Prokaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells do not
Eukaryotic cells have a true, membrane-bound nucleus; prokaryotic cells do not
Prokaryotic cells have mitochondria while eukaryotic cells do not

Which of the following organisms are prokaryotes?
Which organelle in a eukaryotic cell is responsible for producing energy from food?

o: A cell wall made of cellulose, chloroplasts and a large central vacuole

questions.q: What does the nuclear membrane do in a eukaryotic cell?
o: It produces energy for the cell
It surrounds and protects the nucleus, controlling what enters and leaves
It produces proteins for the cell

questions.q: Which of the following correctly describes the size relationship between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
o: Prokaryotic cells are generally 10 to 100 times larger than eukaryotic cells
Eukaryotic cells are generally larger (10–100 µm) than prokaryotic cells (1–10 µm)
Both types are the same size
Size varies too much to make a comparison

questions.q: Blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) are classified as prokaryotes. What evidence supports this?
o: They have no true, membrane-bound nucleus
They are visible to the naked eye

questions.q: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) in a eukaryotic cell is involved in:
o: Protein and lipid production and transport
Converting light energy to chemical energy

The nucleolus is found inside the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell. Its main function is:
o: To produce energy for the nucleus
To store the cell's water content
To produce ribosomal RNA, which is needed to make ribosomes
To control what enters and leaves the nucleus

questions.q: Define a prokaryotic cell and a eukaryotic cell. State the single most important difference between them.
List three features of a prokaryotic cell and describe the function of each.
List five features of a eukaryotic cell and describe the function of each.
Explain what the nucleoid region is in a prokaryotic cell and contrast it with the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell.
What are ribosomes? State whether they are found in prokaryotic cells, eukaryotic cells, or both.
Draw and label a simple prokaryotic cell. Include: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleoid, ribosome and flagellum.
Draw and label a simple animal eukaryotic cell. Include: nucleus, cell membrane, mitochondrion, ribosome and endoplasmic reticulum.
Explain two differences between the cell wall of a bacterium (prokaryote) and the cell wall of a plant cell (eukaryote).
What additional structures would you expect to find in a plant eukaryotic cell that are absent from an animal eukaryotic cell?
Explain why eukaryotic cells are described as more complex than prokaryotic cells.
State three similarities between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

A biologist examines an unknown microorganism under a microscope. She observes: (a) it is very small (about 2 µm), (b) it has a cell wall and a cell membrane, (c) there is no visible nucleus, (d) ribosomes are scattered throughout the cytoplasm. Classify this organism as prokaryotic or eukaryotic and explain your reasoning for each observation.

A student says that because plant cells have a cell wall and bacteria also have a cell wall, plants must be prokaryotes. Explain the error in this student's reasoning and describe the evidence that proves plant cells are eukaryotic.

Cell comparison diagram: Create a large, detailed side-by-side diagram of a prokaryotic cell and a eukaryotic animal cell. Label all visible structures on each. Use colour to distinguish organelles. Add a key below the diagram listing each labelled structure and its function.

Microscope observation: If a microscope is available, observe prepared slides of bacteria (prokaryotic) and cheek cells or onion cells (eukaryotic). Sketch what you see and label the structures visible at your magnification. Note any differences you can observe between the two types.

Cell classification activity: Create a set of 12 organism cards (bacteria, amoeba, grass, mushroom, tree, E. coli, human blood cell, yeast, blue-green algae, onion, cow, and one more of your choice). For each card, state whether it is prokaryotic or eukaryotic and give one piece of evidence to support your classification.

lessons.title: Classifying organisms as prokaryotic or eukaryotic

pages.body:
The bacteria in your gut help you digest food and protect you from harmful microbes. The malaria parasite is a eukaryote that lives inside your blood cells and makes you seriously ill. Some fungi produce antibiotics that save lives. Other fungi cause skin infections. Whether an organism is prokaryotic or eukaryotic affects not just how it looks under a microscope, but how it interacts with our bodies.

- Can you name any organism that causes disease? Is it a prokaryote or a eukaryote?
- Can you name any organism that is beneficial to humans? Is it a prokaryote or a eukaryote?

pages.title: Classifying organisms as prokaryotic or eukaryotic
pages.body:
Every living organism can be classified as either prokaryotic or eukaryotic, based on whether its cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.

Prokaryotes include all bacteria and archaea. Common Ghanaian examples of bacteria include Salmonella typhi (causes typhoid fever), Mycobacterium tuberculosis (causes tuberculosis), Streptococcus (causes throat infections), Vibrio cholerae (causes cholera), Neisseria gonorrhoeae (causes gonorrhoea) and many beneficial soil bacteria that fix nitrogen and decompose organic matter. Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are also prokaryotes and are important for producing oxygen in water bodies.

Eukaryotes include all plants, animals, fungi and protists. Humans, trees, maize, tilapia, cattle, goats, mushrooms and yeast are all eukaryotes. Importantly, several disease-causing organisms are eukaryotes. Plasmodium falciparum (the malaria parasite) is a eukaryotic protist. Candida (a fungus that causes thrush and other infections) is a eukaryote. Trypanosoma (causes sleeping sickness) is a eukaryotic protist.

lessons.title: Impact of prokaryotes on human health

pages.title: Impact of prokaryotes on human health
pages.body: Bacteria cause many of Ghana's most serious diseases. Tuberculosis (TB), caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is a major public health problem in Ghana. Cholera, caused by Vibrio cholerae, is transmitted through contaminated water and food and causes severe diarrhoea. Typhoid fever, caused by Salmonella typhi, spreads through contaminated water and leads to high fever and abdominal pain. Food poisoning is often caused by Salmonella, Staphylococcus or Campylobacter bacteria in contaminated food. Gonorrhoea, a sexually transmitted infection, is caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae.

However, not all prokaryotes are harmful. Many are essential and beneficial. Lactobacillus bacteria in the gut help digest food and prevent harmful bacteria from colonising the intestine. Rhizobium bacteria in soil fix atmospheric nitrogen into forms plants can use, improving soil fertility. Bacteria are used in making yoghurt, cheese and fermented foods such as kenkey and koko. Some bacteria produce antibiotics naturally. Bacteria are used in biotechnology to produce insulin and vaccines.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Impact of eukaryotes on human health

pages.title: Impact of eukaryotes on human health
pages.body:
Eukaryotic pathogens are also significant in Ghana. Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite that causes malaria, is a eukaryote transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito. It reproduces inside human red blood cells, causing the cyclical fevers, anaemia and, in severe cases, death that characterise malaria. Malaria remains Ghana's leading cause of illness and death.

Fungal diseases (caused by eukaryotic fungi) include ringworm, athlete's foot, candidiasis and others. These are more common in warm, humid climates like Ghana's. Some eukaryotic worms — such as roundworms, hookworms and tapeworms — are intestinal parasites that cause malnutrition and anaemia in children. The Trypanosoma protist causes sleeping sickness, transmitted by the tsetse fly.
Beneficial eukaryotes include plants (all food crops are eukaryotes), fungi used in bread-making and brewing, and beneficial gut protozoa that help with digestion.

lessons.title: Safety measures to protect against harmful organisms

pages.title: Safety measures to protect against harmful organisms
pages.body:
Understanding whether a harmful organism is a prokaryote or a eukaryote matters for treatment. Bacterial (prokaryotic) infections can be treated with antibiotics — these work specifically against bacterial cells and do not harm human eukaryotic cells. Antibiotics do NOT work against fungal or protist infections. Fungal infections require antifungal medicines; malaria requires antimalarial drugs such as artemisinin.

Safety measures against harmful prokaryotes include: drinking clean, boiled or treated water to prevent cholera and typhoid; washing hands thoroughly with soap before eating and after using the toilet; cooking food thoroughly to kill bacteria; proper food storage to prevent bacterial growth; getting vaccinated against bacterial diseases such as tuberculosis; and practising safe sex to prevent sexually transmitted bacterial infections.

Safety measures against harmful eukaryotes include: using insecticide-treated bed nets and indoor spraying to prevent malaria; wearing shoes to prevent hookworm infection; washing fruits and vegetables before eating; treating drinking water; deworming children regularly; and proper treatment of fungal skin infections with antifungal creams.

> **Lesson 2 Assessment**

questions.q: Plasmodium falciparum, the malaria parasite, is classified as:
o: A prokaryote, because it is a single-celled organism
A prokaryote, because it lacks a cell wall
A eukaryote, because it has a membrane-bound nucleus
A virus, because it reproduces inside human cells

questions.q: Which of the following is a prokaryote that causes a serious disease in Ghana?
Why can antibiotics treat bacterial infections but NOT malaria?
o: Antibiotics are not strong enough to kill large organisms
Antibiotics specifically target bacterial (prokaryotic) cells; the malaria parasite is a eukaryote not affected by antibiotics
Malaria is a virus so it cannot be killed by any medicine
Antibiotics only work in the gut, not in the blood

questions.q: Which of the following is a beneficial prokaryote?

Ringworm and athlete's foot are caused by which type of organism?

o: Boiling or treating drinking water and washing hands before eating

questions.q: Lactobacillus bacteria in the human gut are beneficial because they:

Help digest food and prevent harmful bacteria from colonising the intestine
Fix nitrogen for use by the human body

o: It determines how large the medicine tablet should be
Different medicines target prokaryotic cells (antibiotics) or eukaryotic pathogens (antifungals, antimalarials)separately
Prokaryotes always cause more serious diseases than eukaryotes

questions.q: Which of the following organisms are prokaryotes?
Deworming children is a safety measure against which type of eukaryotic pathogen?
Name three diseases caused by prokaryotic (bacterial) organisms and state the bacterium responsible for each.
Name three diseases caused by eukaryotic organisms and classify each pathogen as a protist, fungus or worm.
Explain why antibiotics cannot be used to treat malaria.
Describe three ways in which prokaryotic bacteria are beneficial to humans.
Describe how Plasmodium falciparum causes disease in humans. At what stage of its life cycle does it damage human cells?
State four safety measures that help prevent bacterial diseases such as cholera and typhoid. Explain why each measure works.
Explain how using insecticide-treated bed nets protects against malaria. Which organism does this measure target?
Classify each of the following as prokaryotic or eukaryotic: Salmonella, Plasmodium, a maize plant, Rhizobium, Candida, a human being, cyanobacteria.
Explain why Lactobacillus bacteria are important for human health, even though they are prokaryotes that live inside the human body.
Describe two ways that knowledge of whether a disease-causing organism is prokaryotic or eukaryotic affects how doctors treat that disease.
Why are children particularly vulnerable to diseases caused by both prokaryotic and eukaryotic pathogens? Suggest two reasons.

A child in a rural community in the Northern Region of Ghana is ill with high fever, chills, anaemia and extreme fatigue. A second child in the same community has severe diarrhoea and vomiting after drinking from an unprotected well. (a) Suggest the most likely disease for each child, stating the pathogen and whether it is prokaryotic or eukaryotic. (b) Suggest the appropriate treatment for each child. (c) Describe two preventive measures that would protect the community against each disease.

A public health officer is designing an education campaign for a village that suffers from both cholera outbreaks and high malaria rates. Explain why the same set of safety measures will NOT protect against both diseases, and suggest specific measures for each.

Disease and organism classification poster: Create a poster for display in your school health centre. The poster should list six diseases common in Ghana and for each show: the disease name, the causative organism, whether it is prokaryotic or eukaryotic, how it is transmitted, and two prevention measures.

Organism classification card sort: Create cards for 15 organisms (including bacteria, protists, fungi, plants and animals). Shuffle the cards and sort them into two groups: prokaryotes and eukaryotes. For each group, sub-sort into harmful, beneficial and neutral. Write a paragraph explaining your most interesting finding.

Community health survey: Interview five adults in your community about two diseases that are common in your area. Ask: what causes the disease? How is it spread? How is it treated? What do they do to prevent it? For each disease they mention, research whether the causative organism is prokaryotic or eukaryotic. Write a brief report on your findings and share with the class.

pages.body:
| **Word** | **What it means** |
|---|---|
| Prokaryote | An organism whose cells lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus (e.g. bacteria) |
| Eukaryote | An organism whose cells have a true, membrane-bound nucleus (e.g. plants, animals, fungi) |
| Nucleus | The membrane-bound control centre of a eukaryotic cell containing the DNA |
| Nucleoid | The region in a prokaryotic cell where the DNA is found, without a surrounding membrane |
| Organelle | A small, specialised structure inside a cell performing a specific function |
| Mitochondrion | An organelle in eukaryotic cells that produces energy through cellular respiration |
| Ribosome | A tiny structure found in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells that makes proteins |
| Cell wall | A rigid outer layer around the cell membrane providing shape and protection |
| Flagellum | A tail-like structure in some prokaryotes used for movement |
| Pathogen | An organism that causes disease |
| Antibiotic | A medicine that kills or inhibits bacteria (prokaryotes); does NOT work on eukaryotes |
| Antifungal | A medicine that kills or inhibits fungi (eukaryotes) |
| Antimalarial | A medicine used to treat malaria, caused by the eukaryotic parasite Plasmodium |
| Cyanobacteria | Blue-green algae; prokaryotic organisms that photosynthesise |
